result:
There is a particular shade of blue that only exists for about twelve minutes after sunrise, when the sky hasn’t decided whether it will be cloudy or clear. I have seen it twice in my life, both times by accident, while looking for something else—keys, a lost thought, the end of a dream. That is how most of the important things arrive: not announced, but slipped through the side door of attention.

We talk about lives as if they were novels, with chapters and climaxes and neat resolutions. But if you actually live inside one, it feels more like weather. Long stretches of ordinary atmosphere—making coffee, folding laundry, the sound of a refrigerator humming—punctuated suddenly by storms or by those strange, still moments when the air seems to hold its breath. The architecture of a person is built less from the big decisions (the move, the job, the vow) and more from the thousands of tiny choices we barely notice: whether to smile at a stranger, whether to stay five more seconds in a doorway, whether to remember or let go.

Language is always trying to catch up. We build museums of words—poems, texts, half-sentences whispered into pillows—hoping to preserve what is essentially motion. Even now, as these sentences form, they are already becoming memory, shifting shape. That is not a failure; it is the nature of being alive. To write is not to capture the blue, but to point in its direction and say: *Look, it was here. I was here. For a moment, we shared the same light.*

What remains is not the record, but the feeling of having paid attention. And that, perhaps, is enough.
